note: Two mute men, grandsons (or, some say, nephews) of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda, lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Whenever he entered the study hall they came in too, sat before the Sages, nodded their heads and moved their lips. Rabbi prayed for them and they were healed, and it turned out they had learned the Mishna, the Sifra, the Sifrei and the entire Talmud.
why: A baraita had said a mute person is exempt from the Temple assembly because he cannot learn. The Gemara brings this case to challenge that: these mute men did learn. Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi then reread the verse as 'that they may teach'.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the two mute men follow him into the study hall, and he prays for their healing.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda
people.about: The grandfather, or by another account the uncle, of the two mute men.

terms.meaning: An early collection of the Sages' legal interpretations of the book of Leviticus.
An early collection of the Sages' legal interpretations of Numbers and Deuteronomy.
Jewish law; here it means the Mishna, the core collection of legal teachings.

note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma went to pay their respects to their teacher Rabbi Yehoshua in Peki'in. He asked what new idea had been taught in the study hall that day. They demurred, saying they were his students and all their learning came from him, but he insisted that a study hall is never without something new. They told him Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had lectured on the assembly verse 'the men, the women and the little ones': men come to learn, women to hear, and the little ones so that those who bring them are rewarded. Rabbi Yehoshua said they had held a fine pearl and tried to keep it from him. They began to report a second teaching of Rabbi Elazar's; the rest of the conversation comes after this excerpt.
why: The Gemara has been discussing who is obliged in the Temple assembly, deriving the exemption of deaf and mute people from that same verse. This baraita brings a homiletic reading of the verse.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: One of two students who visit Rabbi Yehoshua and report the day's lecture.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma
people.about: The other student who visits Rabbi Yehoshua with Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Their teacher, living in Peki'in, who presses them for the new idea taught that day.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: The Sage whose week it was to lecture in the study hall.

terms.meaning: Hakhel: the gathering of the whole people at the Temple on Sukkot after the Sabbatical Year, to hear the Torah read aloud (Deuteronomy 31).
To draw a teaching from a verse by close, creative reading of its words, beyond their plain sense.

flag: The story stops mid-conversation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's second teaching (in AFTER) and Rabbi Yehoshua's closing praise of him (on 3b) belong to the same story but fall outside the STORY segments.

note: Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit went to greet Rabbi Eliezer in Lod, and Rabbi Eliezer asked what new idea had come up in the study hall that day. Rabbi Yosei told him the Sages had taken a vote and decided that in Ammon and Moab the poor man's tithe is separated in the Sabbatical Year. Rabbi Eliezer said to him in anger: Yosei, put out your hands and catch your eyes, and he did. Then Rabbi Eliezer wept, quoted 'The counsel of the Lord is with those who fear Him', and sent word that the Sages need not worry about their vote: he had a tradition from Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, reaching back to Moses at Sinai, that ruled the same way, and he explained the reason. Once he calmed down, he prayed that Rabbi Yosei's eyes return to their place, and they did.
why: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua's students hesitated to tell him Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's new teachings. Its answer is this incident, in which a student who reported a new ruling to his teacher was struck blind.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit
people.about: A student who visits Rabbi Eliezer and reports the Sages' vote.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage living in Lod; the translation also calls him Rabbi Elazar. He strikes Rabbi Yosei's eyes, then restores them.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's teacher, from whom he received the tradition about Ammon and Moab.

terms.meaning: A tenth of the produce given to the poor in certain years of the seven-year cycle.
Every seventh year, when the Land of Israel is left unworked and its produce is ownerless.

terms.term: halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai
terms.meaning: A law the Sages hold was given orally to Moses, with no verse behind it, and handed down teacher to student.
The holy status of the Land of Israel, which brings its special farming laws. The text says the first one, from the conquest after Egypt, held only for its own time.

note: The Angel of Death used to keep company with Rav Beivai bar Abaye. Once he told his agent to bring him Miriam who braided women's hair, and the agent brought Miriam who raised small children instead. Told of the mistake, the agent offered to return her, but the angel said that since she was here she should be counted among the dead. Rav Beivai asked how the agent could take her before her time; he said she had been lighting and sweeping the oven, set the shovel on her foot and was burned, her luck faltered, so he took her. Asked whether they had the right to do this, the angel quoted 'there are those swept away without justice', explained that he keeps such souls until their generation's years are complete, and said the lost years go to a Torah scholar who lets insults pass.
why: Rav Yosef wept at the verse 'there are those swept away without justice', asking whether anyone really dies before his time. The Gemara answers yes and brings this story to show it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who weeps at a verse suggesting people can die without justice.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: A Sage who kept company with the Angel of Death and questions him about a wrongful death.

people.name: Miriam
people.about: Two women of this name: one who braided women's hair, and one who raised babies and was taken by mistake.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time. Here he has agents who do the work for him.
The name of the angel the text says watches over the souls of the dead.

note: The Sages said to Rava that he seemed to escape both curses of the verse: God never hid His face from him, and the authorities took nothing from him. Rava replied that they did not know how many gifts he sent in secret to the house of King Shapur. Even so, the Sages cast their eyes on him. Meanwhile King Shapur's household sent for Rava and imprisoned him. Rava said this bore out the teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that wherever the Sages cast their eyes, the result is either death or poverty.
why: Rav had just taught that anyone who never suffers God hiding His face, or being devoured by others, is not one of the Jewish people. The Sages raise this teaching against Rava, who seemed to be spared both.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose prayers were answered and who seemed safe from the authorities; he is imprisoned by King Shapur's household.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The ruler to whose house Rava secretly sends gifts, and whose household imprisons him.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: An earlier Sage whose saying Rava quotes: where the Sages cast their eyes comes death or poverty.

terms.meaning: From Deuteronomy 31:17: God turning away from the people, so that prayers seem to go unanswered.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.
Cast their eyes on him: looked at him with suspicion or envy, which the text treats as bringing harm.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya was at the Caesar's court when a heretic made a gesture at him meaning: your nation is the one whose Master has turned His face away from it. Rabbi Yehoshua gestured back: His hand is stretched out over us. The Caesar asked what the two had signed, and Rabbi Yehoshua explained both. Then the court asked the heretic what he had gestured and what he got in reply, and he admitted he did not know what Rabbi Yehoshua's gesture meant. They said a man who does not understand what is signed to him has no business signing before the king, and they took him out and killed him.
why: Rav Yosef has just said that even when God hides His face, His hand is stretched out over Israel. This story shows Rabbi Yehoshua giving that same answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage at the Caesar's court who answers a heretic's insult with a gesture of his own.

people.name: the Caesar
people.about: The Roman emperor, who asks Rabbi Yehoshua to explain the exchange.

terms.meaning: The Talmud's word for someone, often of Jewish origin, who rejects the Sages' teachings and argues against them.

note: Rav Kahana hid under the bed of his teacher Rav and heard him chatting and laughing with his wife and then having relations with her. Rav Kahana said aloud that Rav's mouth was like that of a man who had never tasted a cooked dish. Rav said to him: Kahana, get out, this is not proper conduct.
why: Rav had taught that even light talk between a man and his wife before relations is recounted to him at his death. The Gemara challenges this with Rav's own behavior, then answers that such talk is fine when he needs to win his wife's goodwill.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who hides under his teacher's bed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher, whose private talk with his wife his student overhears.

terms.meaning: A polite phrase in the text for having marital relations.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya were traveling and came to a town, where they asked whether there was a Torah scholar they could go and greet. They were told there was one, but he was blind. Rabbi Hiyya told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to stay behind so as not to lower his dignity as Nasi, and offered to go alone. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi took hold of him and went along anyway. As they left, the blind scholar blessed them: you greeted one who is seen but does not see; may you be worthy to greet the One who sees but is not seen. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said to Rabbi Hiyya that he would have kept him from this blessing.
why: Right after this, the visitors ask the blind scholar where his blessing comes from, and he cites Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching that whoever sees Sages in their lifetime will live, explaining why greeting a scholar earns such a reward.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the Nasi, head of the Jewish community, who insists on visiting the blind scholar himself.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: His traveling companion, who wants to spare him the visit for the sake of his dignity.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, a position of great honor.

terms.term: the One Who sees and is not seen
terms.meaning: God, who sees everything but cannot be seen; the blessing wishes them to come before God.

note: Rav Idi traveled three months on the road to reach the study hall and spent only one day there before heading home, so the Sages mocked him as a student for one day. Hurt, he applied to himself the verse 'I am as one that is a laughingstock to his neighbor'. Rabbi Yohanan begged him not to bring punishment on the Sages. Then Rabbi Yohanan went to the study hall and taught that whoever studies Torah even one day a year is credited by Scripture as if he had studied all year.
why: The Gemara follows the blind scholar's teaching on greeting Sages with this account about honoring a scholar; it then applies Rabbi Yohanan's rule to sin as well, citing the spies' forty days that brought forty years of punishment.

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Father of Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi; he made a three-month journey to spend one day in the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who pleads with Rav Idi not to punish the Sages, then teaches in his defense.

terms.meaning: The study hall where Torah was taught; Rav Idi spent one day there each year.

note: Rav Yehuda said that a man named Hananya ben Hizkiya should be remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been suppressed: its words contradicted the words of the Torah. Three hundred barrels of oil were brought up to him, and he sat in an upper room and expounded the book until it was reconciled.
why: The Gemara has just told of a youth burned by fire for expounding the electrum in Ezekiel. A baraita after this gives another reason the Sages sought to suppress the book, the danger shown by that youth, and Hananya ben Hizkiya again defends it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports Hananya ben Hizkiya's work and praises him.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: The man who saved the book of Ezekiel by expounding it in an upper room.

terms.meaning: Withdrawn and hidden away, so that it would no longer be read as part of Scripture.
Interpreted closely, here to show that Ezekiel's laws do not truly contradict the Torah.

note: A youth was reading the book of Ezekiel in his teacher's house and came to understand the electrum, the mysterious radiance in Ezekiel's vision. Fire came out of the electrum and burned him. The Sages then sought to suppress the book of Ezekiel, but Hananya ben Hizkiya said to them: if this one was wise, is everyone wise?
why: The Gemara had asked whether the electrum may be taught at all, given a youth who was burned for it, and answered that his time had not yet come. This baraita tells that incident in full and gives Hananya ben Hizkiya's defense of the book.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: The man who argues against suppressing the book of Ezekiel after the youth's death.

terms.meaning: Hashmal: a shining substance in Ezekiel's vision of the Divine Chariot (Ezekiel 1:27). The Gemara treats understanding it as dangerous.
To withdraw a book and hide it away, so that it would no longer be read as part of Scripture.
The phrase that introduces a baraita, a teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

note: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai was traveling on a donkey with his student Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh riding behind him. Rabbi Elazar asked to be taught a chapter of the Divine Chariot, and his teacher reminded him it may not be taught to one person unless he understands on his own. Rabbi Elazar asked leave to say something he had learned, and Rabban Yohanan got down from the donkey, wrapped himself, and sat on a stone under an olive tree, saying he could not ride while the Divine Presence and the angels were with them. As Rabbi Elazar expounded, fire came down from heaven and surrounded the trees, which broke into song, and an angel called from the fire that this was the very Chariot. Rabban Yohanan kissed him on the head and praised him as one who both expounds well and lives well.
why: The Gemara is discussing the rule that the Divine Chariot may not be taught to a single student unless he understands on his own; this baraita shows that rule at work. It is followed by a parallel scene with Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The teacher, riding ahead on a donkey, who honors his student's teaching of the Chariot.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
people.about: His student, who expounds the Divine Chariot before him on the road.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: Our father Abraham, whom Rabban Yohanan calls happy to have such a descendant.

terms.meaning: Maaseh Merkava: the mystical teaching drawn from Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot, taught only to a select few.
The Shekhina: God's presence as felt in a particular place or moment.
The angels who serve before God.

note: When the story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's teaching reached Rabbi Yehoshua, he was walking with Rabbi Yosei the Priest, and they decided to expound the Divine Chariot as well. Rabbi Yehoshua began. Although it was the summer solstice, the sky filled with clouds, something like a rainbow appeared, and the ministering angels gathered to listen, like people crowding to see a wedding. Rabbi Yosei the Priest told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, who blessed them and their mothers and said he had dreamed of them all seated at Mount Sinai, called by a heavenly voice to great halls set out for them, their students, and their students' students, in the third group.
why: It follows the account of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh expounding the Chariot. The Gemara then checks both stories against a baraita listing which Sages lectured on these matters before which teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who, hearing of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's teaching, expounds the Divine Chariot himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the Priest
people.about: Rabbi Yehoshua's companion on the road, who reports what happened to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Their teacher, who blesses them and tells them his dream of Mount Sinai.

terms.meaning: Maaseh Merkava: the mystical teaching drawn from Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot, taught only to a select few.
The start of the summer season, when the sky in the Land of Israel is normally clear, so clouds were a sign.
Bat kol: a voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God's message reaching people after prophecy ended.
In the dream, the third rank of those invited to welcome the Divine Presence.

note: Four Sages entered the 'orchard', the realm of the Torah's loftiest secrets: Ben Azzai, ben Zoma, Aher, and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva warned the others that when they reached stones of pure marble they must not cry 'Water, water', because one who speaks falsehood will not stand before God. Ben Azzai glimpsed and died; ben Zoma glimpsed and was harmed; Aher 'chopped down the shoots', meaning he became a heretic. Only Rabbi Akiva came out safely.
why: The Gemara has been telling how Sages expounded the Divine Chariot and were rewarded; this account shows the danger of the same pursuit, and the Gemara goes on to tell more about ben Zoma and Aher.

people.name: Ben Azzai
people.about: One of the four who entered the orchard; he glimpsed and died.

people.name: Ben Zoma
people.about: One of the four; he glimpsed and was harmed, which the translation explains as losing his mind.

people.name: Aher
people.about: 'The other', the name given to Elisha ben Avuya; one of the four, he became a heretic.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The senior of the four, who warned the others; the only one who came out safely.

terms.meaning: A figure of speech for the deepest mystical secrets of the Torah, entered in mind or vision.
A figure of speech for becoming a heretic, ruining what had been planted.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya was standing on a step on the Temple Mount when ben Zoma saw him and did not stand up for him. Rabbi Yehoshua asked where his thoughts were. Ben Zoma said he had been gazing at the gap between the upper waters and the lower waters, only three fingers wide, citing the verse about God's spirit hovering over the waters like a dove over its young without touching them. Rabbi Yehoshua told his students: 'Ben Zoma is still outside.'
why: The Gemara has just said ben Zoma glimpsed the divine and was harmed; this incident is brought about his fate. Afterwards the Gemara itself questions his proof, since the hovering verse comes on the first day and the waters were divided on the second.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage with students, standing on the Temple Mount, whom ben Zoma failed to honor.

people.name: Ben Zoma
people.about: A Sage lost in thought about the mysteries of Creation.

terms.meaning: In Genesis, God divides the waters above the sky from the waters below; ben Zoma was contemplating the space between them.
Not yet inside the secret, that is, he had not yet grasped these matters fully.

note: Aher saw the angel Mitatron, who had been permitted to sit and write down Israel's merits. Since he had a tradition that no one sits in heaven, he said: perhaps, Heaven forbid, there are two powers. Mitatron was taken out and struck with sixty rods of fire, asked why he had not stood up when he saw Aher, and given permission to erase Aher's merits. A Divine Voice proclaimed: 'Return, rebellious children', except Aher. Aher said that since he was banished from that world, he would enjoy this one. He solicited a prostitute; she asked if he was not Elisha ben Avuya. He uprooted a radish on Shabbat and gave it to her, and she said: 'He is other.'
why: The Gemara has just said that Aher 'chopped down the shoots', becoming a heretic, and asks what led him there; this is its answer. Afterwards it turns to his exchanges with Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Aher
people.about: 'The other': Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage who became a heretic; the prostitute's words give him the name.

people.name: Mitatron
people.about: An angel permitted to sit in heaven and write Israel's merits.

terms.meaning: The heretical idea that some power other than God rules the world.
A voice from heaven announcing God's will.
The Sabbath, on which uprooting a plant is forbidden; Aher did it openly to show he had abandoned the Torah.

note: After Aher had gone astray he asked Rabbi Meir about a verse comparing wisdom to gold and glass. Rabbi Meir said words of Torah are as hard to acquire as gold and as easy to lose as glass. Aher answered that Rabbi Akiva, Meir's teacher, had read it differently: broken gold and glass vessels can be repaired, so a Torah scholar who has sinned can be repaired too. Rabbi Meir said: then you too, return. Aher said he had already heard from behind the heavenly curtain: 'Return, rebellious children', except Aher.
why: The Gemara is gathering exchanges between Aher and his student Rabbi Meir after Aher went astray; this follows one on another verse, and the refusal it ends with returns in the next story, on the Shabbat ride.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage who had gone astray, still teaching Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who urges him to repent.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Meir's teacher, whose reading of the verse Aher quotes.

terms.meaning: The curtain that hides God from the world; to hear something there is to hear a heavenly decree.

note: Aher was riding a horse on Shabbat while Rabbi Meir walked behind him to learn Torah. Aher told him to turn back, as by his horse's steps they had reached the Shabbat boundary. Meir said: you too, return. Aher said he had heard behind the curtain that he alone was excluded. Meir took hold of him and brought him to a study hall, where Aher asked a child to recite his verse; the verse was about the wicked. So it went in thirteen synagogues. The last child, who stuttered, seemed to say 'And to Elisha God says, what is it for you to declare My statutes'. Some say Aher had a knife and tore the child apart; others say he said that had he a knife, he would have torn him apart.
why: The Gemara is collecting traditions about Aher after he went astray, each turning on his claim that he alone was barred from repentance; it goes on to tell what became of him after death.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Sage turned heretic, who still taught Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who tried to bring him back.

terms.meaning: The distance, about two thousand cubits beyond a town, that one may walk on the Sabbath.
Asking a schoolchild what verse he had just learned, and taking the answer as a sign from heaven.

note: When Aher died, it was said he would be neither judged, because he had studied Torah, nor brought into the World-to-Come, because he had sinned. Rabbi Meir said it was better that he be judged and then brought in, and that when he himself died he would make smoke rise from Aher's grave. When Rabbi Meir died, smoke rose from the grave. Rabbi Yohanan asked whether it was a mighty deed to burn one's teacher, and whether no one could save him; he said that when he died he would put out the smoke. When Rabbi Yohanan died, the smoke stopped, and a eulogizer said: 'Even the guard at the entrance could not stand before you, our rabbi.'
why: The Gemara has told how Aher was barred from repentance in his lifetime; this tells his fate after death. Next it asks how Rabbi Meir could have learned Torah from him at all.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Elisha ben Avuya, a Torah scholar who sinned and became a heretic.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Aher's student, who arranged for him to be judged.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A later Sage who vowed to rescue Aher and, at his death, did.

terms.meaning: The life after death in which the righteous are rewarded.
A sign that the dead man was being judged and punished, as a step before he could enter the World-to-Come.

note: Aher's daughter came to Rabbi and asked him to support her. When she said whose daughter she was, he asked whether any of Aher's offspring were still in the world, quoting a verse that the wicked leave no son or grandson. She said: remember his Torah, not his deeds. At once fire came down and licked Rabbi's bench. Rabbi wept and said that if this is how God protects those who treat the Torah with contempt, how much more so those who honor it.
why: The Gemara is completing its account of Aher; her plea to remember his Torah leads into its next question, how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from such a man, which it answers that one may take the words of a flawed Sage.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the leading Sage, to whom Aher's daughter came for support.

people.name: The daughter of Aher
people.about: Aher's daughter, in need of food, who pleads for her father's memory.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Her father, Elisha ben Avuya, a Torah scholar who became a heretic.

terms.meaning: Used alone, the title refers to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

note: Rabba bar Sheila met Elijah the prophet and asked what God was doing. Elijah said God was repeating teachings in the name of all the Sages, but not in Rabbi Meir's name, because Meir had learned from Aher. Rabba bar Sheila objected: Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the inside and threw away the peel. Elijah replied that now God was saying: 'My son Meir says: when a person suffers, the Divine Presence says, My head is heavy, My arm is heavy. If God grieves so over the blood of the wicked, how much more over the blood of the righteous.'
why: The Gemara has been asking how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from Aher and answering that a scholar can take the good and leave the rest, like a date or a nut; this story shows heaven accepting that defense.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: A Sage who met Elijah and defended Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who reports to Rabba bar Sheila what God is doing.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who learned from Aher; God at first will not quote him.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, pictured studying and quoting the teachings of the Sages.

terms.meaning: God's presence in the world, the Shekhina, here pictured as feeling a sufferer's pain.
Rulings of Jewish law.

note: Yehuda ben Tabbai had a false witness executed, to counter the Sadducees, who held such witnesses are executed only if their victim was executed. Shimon ben Shatah told him he had shed innocent blood, since the Sages taught that false witnesses are executed only when both are proven false. At once Yehuda ben Tabbai resolved never to rule on law except in Shimon ben Shatah's presence. All his life he lay on the executed man's grave, and his voice could be heard. People thought it was the dead man's voice. He said it was his own, and that they would know it when he died, for then the voice would no longer be heard.
why: The mishna lists the pairs of Sages who led the Sanhedrin, and Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree over which of these two was the head; the Gemara asks which view this account follows, since it has Yehuda ben Tabbai ruling in front of Shimon ben Shatah.

people.name: Yehuda ben Tabbai
people.about: A Sage who had a false witness executed and spent his life in penance for it.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: His colleague, who told him he had shed innocent blood.

terms.meaning: A witness proven to have given false testimony to harm someone; the Torah gives him the penalty he tried to bring on his victim.
A Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected many traditions of the Sages.
A form of oath: may I not see Israel's consolation if what I say is not true.

note: Alexa died in Lod, and all of Israel gathered to eulogize him. Rabbi Tarfon would not let them, because it was the Festival of Shavuot. The text tells nothing more about Alexa or the funeral.
why: The mishna allowed eulogies and fasts on the day after Shavuot to reject the Sadducee view that Shavuot always falls on a Sunday; this incident seems to contradict it. The Gemara reads it as the day after the Festival, and says that day is festive only when Shavuot does not fall on Shabbat.

people.name: Alexa
people.about: A man who died in Lod, whom all Israel came to eulogize.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who forbade the eulogy because of the Festival.

terms.meaning: The Festival of Weeks, one of the three pilgrimage festivals, fifty days after Passover.
To mourn the dead publicly with a funeral speech, which is not done on a festival.

flag: The story is a single sentence, quoted inside a legal objection; it has an event but almost no narrative.

note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok told of two women, both married to men who kept the purity laws strictly, whose clothes were switched at the bathhouse. The case came before Rabbi Akiva, and he declared the clothes impure.
why: Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram has just ruled that clothes become impure if their owner wore them mistaking them for others, because his attention lapsed; this incident supports him. Rabbi Oshaya then objects that by that logic any mix-up would make food impure.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who ruled the switched clothes impure.

terms.meaning: 'Associates': people committed to keeping the laws of ritual purity strictly, even for ordinary food.
Ritually impure: unfit for contact with pure food or holy things until purified. It is a religious status, not dirt.

note: A woman came to Rabbi Yishmael and said she had woven a garment while ritually pure, though she had not set her mind on keeping it pure. As he questioned her, she mentioned that a menstruating woman had pulled the rope with her. Rabbi Yishmael said: how great are the words of the Sages, who said that if one's mind is on guarding an item, it is pure, and if not, it is impure.
why: The Gemara is challenging rulings that clothes become impure when their owner mistakes them for others; Rabba bar Avuh raises this case to show that what counts is whether one meant to guard the item, not whether one knew what it was.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman brought a question about her weaving.

terms.meaning: Under the purity laws a woman during her period is ritually impure and can make things she moves impure.
Fit for contact with pure food or holy things; a religious status, not cleanliness.

note: Another woman came to Rabbi Yishmael and said she had woven a cloth while ritually pure, though she had not set her mind on guarding it. As he questioned her, she said a thread had snapped and she had tied it with her mouth. Rabbi Yishmael said: how great are the words of the Sages, who said that if one's mind is on guarding an item, it is pure, and if not, it is impure.
why: This is the second of the cases Rabba bar Avuh raises against the rulings on switched clothes. The Gemara then reconciles Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's case: each wife assumed the other was married to an unlearned man and stopped guarding her clothes.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman brought a question about her weaving.

terms.meaning: Saliva wet the thread; under the purity laws a liquid readily takes on impurity and passes it to the cloth.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua said he was ashamed of Beit Shammai's ruling: could a woman and her bowl be impure for seven days while the dough she kneads in it stays pure? A student of Beit Shammai offered to explain. He got Rabbi Yehoshua to agree that an impure vessel does not block impurity and that an unlearned man's vessel is impure, then said: if you tell such a man his vessel is impure, will he listen? He will say, 'Mine is pure and yours is impure.' At once Rabbi Yehoshua went and lay on the graves of Beit Shammai and said: 'I humble myself before you, bones of Beit Shammai.' It was said that all his life his teeth were dark from his fasts.
why: The mishna records Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel arguing over what stays pure in a room with a corpse; this story gives Beit Shammai's reasoning, from which the Gemara concludes that the purity of the unlearned man's vessels matters to the observant as well.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who mocked Beit Shammai's ruling and then did penance for it.

people.name: A student of Beit Shammai
people.about: An unnamed student who explained the school's reasoning to Rabbi Yehoshua.

terms.meaning: The school of the Sage Shammai, whose rulings often differ from those of the school of Hillel.
Literally 'people of the land': someone who does not keep the purity laws carefully, so his things are treated as impure.
The impurity a corpse passes on, which takes a week-long purification.
A sealed vessel that stops corpse impurity spreading to what is beyond it.

note: A man was carrying a barrel of sacrificial wine from place to place. The strap of his sandal, which had become impure from being trodden on by a zav, broke off. He picked it up and laid it on the mouth of the barrel; it fell into the barrel's airspace and made the wine impure. At that time the Sages declared that one carrying an object trodden by a zav may carry teruma with it, but not sacrificial food.
why: The mishna allows carrying teruma, but not sacrificial food, alongside an object trodden by a zav, and the Gemara asks why sacrificial food is different; this incident is the answer. It then asks why the rule was not extended to teruma.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Yehuda reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A man with a certain bodily discharge; he is ritually impure, and anything he treads or sits on becomes impure too.
The portion of produce given to priests; holy, but less so than food from Temple offerings.
Food from Temple offerings, which has the strictest purity rules.
An earthenware vessel becomes impure when an impure thing enters the space inside it, even without touching its contents.

note: A man was carrying the water and ashes used for purification across the Jordan in a boat. An olive-sized piece of a corpse was then found stuck in the floor of the boat. At that time the Sages declared that no one may carry the water and ashes of purification across the Jordan in a boat.
why: Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya held that a decree prompted by an incident covers only that incident's exact circumstances, the Jordan and a boat; this is that incident. The Gemara uses his view to explain why the sandal decree applies to sacrificial food and not teruma.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Yehuda reports the incident.

terms.meaning: Water mixed with ashes of the red heifer, sprinkled to purify people and things impure from contact with the dead.
A piece the size of an olive, the smallest amount of a corpse that makes things impure.
